Sampled HR@10 measures ranking against the specified 99 negatives, not full-catalog HR@10; sampled metrics can even reverse model rankings. Preserve the pinned evaluator, users, unique candidates, and seeds across comparisons, and describe gains as specific to this benchmark protocol. Fixed candidates remove candidate-resampling noise from model differences but do not establish full-catalog superiority. [Krichene & Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

Recommended adaptation of [paired bootstrap resampling](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/): retain each model’s per-user binary hit indicators; resample 200 users with replacement independently within each category, using identical sampled indices for both models. For each of roughly 10,000 replicates, compute four category differences and their equal-weight macro-average; report the observed difference and a 95% percentile interval. One changed hit is 0.5 percentage points within a category, or 0.125 points in the four-category macro-average. These intervals quantify user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the candidates and trained models; they exclude training-seed and candidate-sampling variability. Resampling saved predictions requires no additional training.

Repeated hyperparameter and checkpoint selection can overfit validation noise; an ordinary bootstrap interval after selecting the winner does not correct that selection bias. [Cawley & Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html). Practical recommendations: predeclare trial limits, checkpoint evaluation frequency, stopping and tie-breaking rules; log all attempted configurations and inspected checkpoints; select using the required macro HR@10 while reporting category results and paired gains against the baseline. Treat tiny gains and intervals spanning zero as inconclusive. Keep test labels inaccessible throughout search and freeze the complete selection before the host’s final held-out evaluation.
